summary: Provides background information for the Internet Accounting Architecture, a way to measure network usage. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains a model for measuring network traffic and reporting the results. It focuses on how to collect useful information while limiting cost and protecting sensitive data.

subtitle: Background on measuring and reporting network use across administrative boundaries.

tldr.problem: Network providers and users may need to understand traffic use, check policy compliance or allocate costs, but measuring and protecting detailed data adds overhead.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes meters that count flows, collectors that protect and transport the results, and applications that process and store them.
tldr.outcome: This Informational background document focuses on usage reporting and leaves billing, enforcement and several design decisions outside its scope.

today: RFC 1272 is an Informational memo published in November 1991, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo says its companion architecture and meter-service documents were still under construction.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1272 is the background document in a planned set of three documents about Internet accounting. The architecture and meter-service documents were still under construction when this memo was published. Its immediate focus is the meaning, format and reporting of network-usage measurements.

The memo limits its goal to usage reporting. It does not recommend billing practices or specify how reports should enforce network policy. It also identifies the work as a short-term effort intended to fit with the developing OSI and Autonomous Network Research Group work.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo explains how a network might measure and report traffic use. It does not decide who pays or how a provider enforces its rules.

sections.title: Reasons to Measure Usage
sections.content:
The memo gives three reasons to report usage: subscribers can understand their network behavior, providers can measure compliance with stated limits, and organizations can allocate or recover costs. A report by itself does not enforce a policy; it can show whether other enforcement methods may be needed.

Measurement has costs. Counting and collecting data uses computing resources and network capacity, while storing and analyzing reports also takes work. More detailed and reliable measurements increase these costs, so the memo recommends collecting only the detail needed for a particular purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: Usage reports can help people understand traffic, check agreed limits and allocate costs. Collect only the detail needed, because measuring and storing more information takes resources.

sections.title: Meters, Collectors and Applications
sections.content:
The memo adopts a three-part accounting model. A meter measures traffic and combines measurements into totals. A collector protects meter data while it is stored or moved in the short term. An application processes, formats and stores the collected data.

The proposed work concentrates on meters and collectors, with less attention to applications. The model assumes an administrator measures traffic within an administrative domain and traffic crossing its boundaries. It treats directly connected administrative domains as the relevant neighbors for accounting.
sections.plainLanguage: A meter counts traffic, a collector keeps the counts safe as they move, and an application uses the results. Each network administrator is mainly concerned with traffic inside their domain and traffic exchanged with neighboring domains.

sections.title: Meter Placement and Detail
sections.content:
A meter examines packets and records aggregate counts for flows between communicating entities. Complete accuracy requires examining every packet, while statistical sampling may be sufficient when the required accuracy is lower. The memo identifies routers as a generally convenient location because they sit at network boundaries, concentrate traffic and can see adjacent systems.

It lists network monitors, line monitors, meters built into routers and router spiders made from line monitors. The amount of detail can vary by entity, packet attribute, recorded value and reporting interval. Each combination creates a separate meter and uses memory.
sections.plainLanguage: Meters count traffic flows, often at routers near network boundaries. Counting more kinds of traffic in more detail needs more memory and reporting capacity.

sections.title: Protecting and Collecting the Data
sections.content:
The memo identifies confidentiality, data integrity, and local and remote control as collection concerns. Usage information can reveal subscriber behavior, so the collector should protect it during collection, storage and delivery. The memo assumes that SNMP mechanisms might provide these services, but says further investigation is needed.

Reliable delivery could use acknowledgments and retransmissions, reports to multiple collectors, or backup storage at the meter. Polling lets a collector control when meters send data but adds network overhead. The memo leaves open whether traffic should be counted as it enters or exits a router, while requiring that either choice be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Usage data can be sensitive, so the collection system should protect it and avoid losing it. The memo leaves the choice of counting packets on router entry or exit to the network administrator.
